 The Wild Are Getting Healthy and Becoming A Nightmare For the NHL
 The Wild Are Getting Healthy and Becoming A Nightmare For the NHL 
 Image courtesy of Bruce Kluckhohn-Imagn Images
 By 
 Chris Schad 
 - 13 hours ago 
 It’s been hard for Minnesota Wild fans not to feel excited lately. The Wild entered Wednesday with an eight-point lead over the Dallas Stars in the Central Division and are only one point behind the Edmonton Oilers for the Western Conference top spot. 
 The Wild inspired more optimism on Tuesday night when they handed the Nashville Predators a 7-3 beatdown at home. Brock Faber had returned from a fractured skull. Matt Boldy almost potted his second hat trick in a week. Quinn Hughes is playing like he wants another Hart Trophy, and Kirill Kaprizov is the best player in the NHL right now, not named Connor McDavid or Leon Draisaitl . 
 In short, you can’t blame a Wild fan for feeling good in Grand Casino Arena on any given night. And the biggest reason to be excited is that this team hasn’t reached its final form. 
 The Wild began the season working things out on the fly. Head coach John Hynes was tasked with finding a solution after Minnesota lost 150 points in free agency with the departures of Marcus Johansson , Vladimir Tarasenko , and Mats Zuccarello . While they were high on Maxim Shabanov , Blake Coleman , and Bobby Brink to fill those roles, nobody really knew who would step up or where they would ultimately fall in the lineup. 
 The questions ran deeper at goaltender. Filip Gustavsson , who had been the Wild’s 1A to Jesper Wallstedt ’s 1B last season, underwent hip surgery that would keep him out for the first two months of the season. Wallstedt showed he could carry the load as the primary netminder through Minnesota’s playoff run last year, but nobody really knew how much he could play or how effective he would be. 
 Then there were the injuries. Faber’s fractured skull was the most serious of the group and ignited a blue line shuffle that lasted through the first two months. Olli Maatta and Jared Spurgeon also missed time, leaving replacements like Daemon Hunt , David Spacek , and Matt Kiersted with bigger roles early in the year. 
 With a road-heavy schedule, it would have been understandable if the Wild needed a minute to get going. But they banked wins thanks to a little creativity. 
 Hynes jump-started the Wild’s offense by pairing Matt Boldy, Joel Eriksson Ek , and Kirill Kaprizov on the top line. While some viewed this as making Minnesota a top-heavy team, the line has been dominant and hadn’t been scored on until Tuesday’s win over the Predators. 
 Meanwhile, the remaining three lines don’t have many concerns. Shabanov looks like a power-play demon. Brink hasn’t scored as much as Wild fans hoped, but brings a defensive grittiness that’s perfect for the bottom six. Even Marcus and Nick Foligno ’s return on the fourth line adds muscle, and it all came together in a seven-goal explosion. 
 That’s not the only thing Wild fans can grab onto.  
 Faber came back much sooner than the worst-case scenario, and any concerns about his fitness disappeared as soon as he laced up his skates. In two games , Faber has a goal, an assist, and a plus-4 rating. Meanwhile, the rest of the defensive pairings are back in place, with Spurgeon and  Jonas Brodin  together and Bogosian and Maatta playing on the third line once Maatta returns from  injured reserve. 
 The goaltending has also been strong. Wallstedt has been playing at a level that could make him the Vezina Trophy favorite, posting a record of 15-2-3 with a .924 save percentage and a 1.99 goals-against average. While there's some concern about burnout after 20 starts following 35 regular-season games a year ago, Gustavsson could be nice insurance as he  begins a conditioning stint with the Iowa Wild this week. 
 With that, the roster feels complete. But another move could be on the horizon to make this team better. Dylan Larkin feels like a pipe dream as the Detroit Red Wings are  reportedly holding him hostage. But acquiring another center or a wing could make this team even deeper and put them in the best position to win a Stanley Cup in franchise history. 
 All of that means the Wild are still an unfinished product, and that’s an exciting thought for fans and a terrifying one for the rest of the NHL. 
 By 
 Chris Schad
